tx.t: This morning we are going to look at some basic facts about the Moon. The Moon is about three hundred and eighty-four thousand kilometres from the Earth.
It takes about twenty-seven days to orbit the Earth once. The same side of the Moon always faces us, because its rotation takes exactly as long as its orbit.
The Moon is about a quarter of the width of the Earth. Gravity on the Moon is only about one-sixth of gravity on Earth.
In nineteen sixty-nine, Apollo Eleven became the first mission to land humans there.

tx.t: In this lecture I will describe the world's rainforests and why scientists want to protect them. Rainforests cover only about six per cent of the Earth's land surface.
However, they are home to more than half of all the plant and animal species on land. The Amazon is the largest rainforest, and it spreads across nine countries.
A rainforest has four main layers: the emergent layer, the canopy, the understorey and the forest floor. Most animals live in the canopy, where there is plenty of light and fruit.
Many modern medicines come from rainforest plants, and scientists believe thousands more are still unknown.

tx.t: Today I will outline how solar power works and why its use is growing. Solar panels contain photovoltaic cells, which turn sunlight directly into electricity.
Most cells are made of silicon, the second most common element in the Earth's crust. The first practical silicon solar cell was made at Bell Laboratories in nineteen fifty-four.
A typical modern panel converts about twenty per cent of the sunlight that hits it into electricity. Over the last decade the cost of panels has fallen by about ninety per cent.
A panel usually works for about twenty-five years, although its output slowly declines.

tx.t: In this talk I will explain what psychologists know about memory and how students can use it. In eighteen eighty-five, the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus described the forgetting curve.
He found that people forget roughly half of new material within an hour if they do not review it. In nineteen fifty-six, George Miller suggested that short-term memory holds about seven items.
Reviewing material at increasing intervals, which is called spaced repetition, helps to move it into long-term memory. Testing yourself is more effective than simply reading your notes again.
A good night of sleep after studying helps to store what you have learned.

In eighteen sixty-six, the population was about six thousand. Over the next fifty years it grew to fifteen thousand.
Then things changed, because the railway came and brought cheaper goods from the cities. As a result, many small traders went out of business.
